Italian army paratroopers patrol the streets of Milan, on Saturday, ahead of an expected protest against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services [AP Photo/Antonio Calanni]By Michele BertelliPublished On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
Milan, Italy – Protests have been called in eight Italian cities on Saturday to demonstrate against Giorgia Meloni’s right-wing government and the rising cost of living, a week after demonstrations in Milan spiralled into clashes with police and looting.
It follows the announcement online of a new round of protests by a newly formed group calling itself the ‘October 17 Movement’, which has been the main driver of demonstrations alongside student federations, grassroots trade unions, and antiwar coalitions.

“Those who deny our future are truly violent,” it said on Instagram. “We distrust this government because we see it as authoritarian.”
In response to last weekend’s looting, the government announced a series of new security measures, including the deployment of 500 soldiers to Italy’s financial hub.
On Friday morning, police carried out inspections in several cities, the Italian news agency Adnkronos reported. Officers carried out another round of more than 150 inspections on Saturday morning in the northern region of Lombardy.

item.title: Do abstaining voters hold the key to Brazil’s 2026 presidential election?
item.description:
Can abstaining voters shake up Brazil's presidential election?
An estimated 33.4 million voters did not cast a ballot in Brazil's general election, the highest rate in decades. How might they affect the run-off?Supporters of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro rally in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 18 [Andre Penner/AP Photo]Supporters of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro rally in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 18 [Andre Penner/AP Photo]By Euan MarshallPublished On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
SaveShare Do abstaining voters hold the key to Brazil’s 2026 presidential election? on social mediashare-nodes
Sharefacebook

Sao Paulo, Brazil – The first time she voted in a Brazilian presidential election, in 2014, Larissa Campelo voted for centre-right Senator Aecio Neves. Four years later, in the next presidential race, she supported a centre-left candidate, former Sao Paulo Mayor Fernando Haddad.
But ahead of what is expected to be one of Brazil’s tightest presidential run-offs ever, the 30-year-old mother of one has decided she has had enough with politics.
She is abstaining from the vote on Sunday, just as she did during the first round of the election on October 4.
Voting is compulsory for most Brazilian adults. But Campelo is part of a historically large chunk of the electorate sitting out this year's presidential race.
Some 33.4 million Brazilian adults did not show up to vote in the first round, resulting in a 21 percent abstention rate, the highest for a general election since 1998.
“It’s my form of protest. I don’t want to dirty my hands with these candidates,” said Campelo, who lives in the Sao Paulo city of Araraquara.
“This isn’t apathy. It’s because I don’t feel there’s anyone qualified enough to earn my vote.”
But appealing to abstaining voters like Campelo may prove to be a path to victory in Sunday's run-off.

Crowds at a petrol station in Port Sudan [File: Fatima Edam/Al Jazeera]By Fatima EdamPublished On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
Azhari Mohamed drives his minibus and eight passengers seven times a day from the Shagar neighbourhood in the Port of Sudan to the city centre and back again.
But despite the long hours – working from 6am to 9pm – fuel shortages in the city have made it difficult for the 60-year-old to make a living.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Drone strike on Abyei market near Sudan-South Sudan border kills 150list 2 of 3Drone attack in disputed Sudan-South Sudan border region kills at least 153list 3 of 3How Sudan’s shift to drone warfare is fuelling a civilian crisisend of list
Azhari’s minibus uses three gallons (11 litres) of petrol a day, costing him about 105,000 Sudanese pounds ($11.30 a day, according to Sudan’s parallel-market exchange rate). With fuel increasingly difficult to obtain, he now spends two days on the road and a third day queuing for fuel.
He can spend more than five hours waiting in line when he needs to fill the tank of his minibus and often finds petrol has run out before his turn comes. When that happens, he goes to the back of the queue at another petrol station hoping to fill up there.
The shortages have led to price rises with a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol now costing 40,000 Sudanese pounds ($4.30) in Gazira State, south of Khartoum, while in Port Sudan it is 35,000 pounds ($3.80) a gallon.
“We can no longer work because of the fuel shortages. The transport fares are no longer enough to cover the cost of running the vehicle and our household expenses,” Azhari told Al Jazeera.
He says the long hours spent queueing for petrol is time he could spend earning money to support his family.

A shattered window at Saint George’s Greek Orthodox Church, where gunmen opened fire during a funeral the previous day, in the village of Hamoud, Karak, Jordan, October 24 [Alaa Al Sukhni/Reuters]By Mariem BahPublished On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
Security forces in Jordan are searching for three gunmen who opened fire at a church in Karak governorate on Friday, killing eight people and injuring dozens more, according to Jordan’s Ministry of Health.
King Abdullah II said those behind the attack would face the “harshest penalties”, as he offered his condolences to the victims’ families. He has ordered a review of the country’s security procedures for responding to terrorist attacks.

Authorities are calling this rare attack on a Christian place of worship an act of terror, with the perpetrators yet to be identified.
Here’s what we know about how the attack unfolded, and what was behind it.
What happened during the church shooting in Karak?
On Friday afternoon, three masked gunmen opened fire during a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud.
Survivors said they heard an explosion just after the start of the service. Two attackers who arrived in a vehicle were joined by a third carrying a semi-automatic rifle. They entered the church and opened fire for several minutes.
One survivor, Nasser al-Burqan, a lawyer, told the Reuters news agency that one of the attackers, standing about two metres (6.5 feet) away, pointed a handgun at him and opened fire.
